children: The latest U.S. labor-market data provided further signs of weak labor demand, with August job openings falling to a five-month low and a September measure of households' views on jobs dropping to a post-Covid low, Pantheon Macroeconomics said.
Data released on Tuesday provided further signs that August's 162K jump in payrolls was a false dawn for the labor market, according to Pantheon economists Samuel Tombs and Oliver Allen.
The August JOLTS report showed job openings retreating to 7,079K from 7,335K, below the 7,228K consensus forecast.
Pantheon said the decline in JOLTS openings closes some of the gap between the series and alternative measures from Indeed and LinkUp, which it considers a more reliable guide to labor demand.

Indeed and LinkUp are based on counts of jobs listed online, while JOLTS openings are based on a survey whose response rate has fallen sharply recently. The collective message, Pantheon said, is that labor demand remains stuck at a relatively depressed level.

That message was echoed by September's Conference Board consumer survey. The net percentage of households reporting that jobs were plentiful rather than difficult to come by fell to 1.7% from 4.2% in August, a post-Covid low.
Pantheon said the jobs differential had been a remarkably good guide to initial estimates of private payrolls from 2022 to 2025 but has painted too downbeat a picture recently.

Other reliable hiring indicators also point to payroll growth remaining very weak in the fall, Pantheon said. The economists reiterated their forecast for a below-consensus 60K increase in September nonfarm payrolls, comprising a 50K gain in private payrolls and a 10K rise in government jobs.
They also expect continued weakness in payrolls over the following few months to put renewed upward pressure on the unemployment rate.

title: Latest data show more signs of weak U.S. labor demand
